We address this by approximating viscosity solutions using physics-informed neural networks within a policy iteration scheme with a vanishing-viscosity annealing schedule. Theoretically, we establish an explicit $\varepsilon$-Nash guarantee by bounding per-player regret via computable residuals and prove our method reaches this stopping criterion in finite time. For two-player zero-sum games, we further establish a computable bound on the approximation error of the value function. Numerical experiments on pursuit-evasion scenarios illustrate the tightness of these computed bounds and the framework's scalability to high-dimensional environments.
authors: Takuma Adams, Andrew C. Cullen, Tansu Alpcan

title: Pretraining for Forecasting in Relational Databases
summary: arXiv:2611.33645v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Real-world forecasting increasingly relies on asynchronous transaction logs in relational databases rather than uniformly sampled arrays. While relational deep learning (RDL) models can forecast from these complex histories, they are typically trained separately for each specific target and root entity type. We introduce Query-Conditioned Relational pretraining (QCRP), a self-supervised framework that enables a standard RDL backbone to act as a universal forecaster across a database. QCRP generates diverse forecasting objectives using a structured temporal query grammar and interleaves them through a shared conditional predictor. This produces a robust, frozen encoder reusable for downstream tasks via lightweight predictors or a zero-shot interface. Evaluated on large-scale RelBench databases, QCRP learns frozen representations that support competitive forecasting across tasks and entity types. Furthermore, a single unified QCRP model checkpoint is competitive with isolated, entity-specific specialists. We demonstrate promising results for reusing the learned representations from standard RDL backbones for forecasting tasks in relational databases.
authors: Ziyue Lin, Sebastian Regalado Lozano, Michael Guerzhoy, Ricardo Baptista, George Stein

title: The Danger of Double Precision: Working Precision as a Hidden Constraint in Gaussian Process Maximum Likelihood
summary: arXiv:2611.33647v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Gaussian process (GP) hyperparameters are routinely fitted by maximizing the marginal likelihood in IEEE double precision, although for smooth kernels and noiseless data the covariance matrix is often more ill conditioned than double precision can resolve. For a squared-exponential kernel on a design with a Bayesian-optimization cluster, refits over a range of significand widths, judged against a high-precision reference, show that the double-precision fit is a different model and that fits converge only once the width exceeds the base-2 logarithm of the covariance condition number, about 70 bits. Cholesky failure acts as an implicit conditioning constraint, caused mostly by rounding of the kernel entries; the constrained solution predicted from the working precision alone is within 20% of the best Powell fits at five of the six precisions from 40 to 64 bits, with a local expansion proved for the idealized problem. Across 43 kernels, designs and problem settings, including negative controls that double precision already resolves, the bits needed follow the log condition number at the reference optimum plus a tolerance-dependent offset, and at the loosest tolerance double precision suffices for the Matern 1.5 kernel but not for the squared-exponential kernel on clustered designs. Double-precision hyperparameters overstate the posterior standard deviation near the design cluster and, on a quadratic objective whose likelihood heads to the flat limit, stall closed-loop active learning. Promoting the whole likelihood to 80 significand bits recovers the reference accuracy on every fixed design tested, whereas a fixed jitter trades failures for a posterior bias.
authors: Thomas A. Scott

title: PRIOR: Pre-Call Reasoning in SFT and Its Influence on Tool-Use Retention under RL
summary: arXiv:2611.33648v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Tool use learned during supervised fine-tuning (SFT) is not always retained during reinforcement learning (RL). We study how properties of SFT data may affect this retention by constructing Low, Medium, and High SFT datasets with approximately matched token budgets but different tool-call depths. Under the same RL recipe, the three initializations reach similar RL training accuracy yet exhibit markedly different tool-use dynamics: tool initiation increases in Low, declines in Medium, and collapses in High. We observe that these datasets also differ substantially in the amount of reasoning preceding each tool call. In particular, High trajectories contain considerably less pre-call reasoning, motivating the hypothesis that pre-call reasoning may affect how well tool use is calibrated and, consequently, whether the corresponding behaviors are retained during RL. An idealized theoretical analysis provides a selective-retention view of this process: advantages in overall and tool-conditioned accuracy can be preserved under outcome-only optimization, while tool initiation increases only when tool-using trajectories are more successful than the tool-free alternative. Guided by this analysis, we rank the original High trajectories by average pre-call reasoning length and retain the highest-ranked examples while approximately matching cumulative SFT token exposure. This simple filtering strategy improves post-RL accuracy and tool-conditioned final-answer success without consistently increasing tool initiation across multiple benchmarks. These results suggest that pre-call reasoning is a useful dimension of SFT supervision for understanding and improving tool-use retention under downstream RL.
authors: Kaiwen Hu, Hyunin Lee, Joseph Suh, Serina Chang, Shuai Shao, Yong Zhang, Namyong Park, Xiaoqiang Luo, Luke Simon, Somayeh Sojoudi

title: Self-supervised Clipped-objective Reinforcement Leaning Framework for Risk-aware Portfolio Management
summary: arXiv:2611.33652v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Portfolio management involves balancing diverse financial assets, a critical yet challenging task in quantitative trading. Although deep reinforcement learning has emerged as an active research domain for solving complex sequential decision-making problems over the past decade, deploying reinforcement learning frameworks in non-stationary financial markets raises formidable difficulties. Most existing reinforcement learning-based portfolio management models fail to account for tick-level intraday market dynamics (e.g., order flow imbalances and liquidity fluctuations), which reflect rapid capital movements. Simultaneously, these models suffer from unstable learning processes due to reinforcement learning's inherent high variance. This paper presents a Self-supervised Clipped-objective Portfolio management framework (SCP), which addresses these limitations through a two-phase architecture. Market feature integration phase (application contribution) integrates micro-level market microstructure patterns with macro-level financial indicators to enhance sensitivity to intraday asset trend dynamics. Policy optimization Phase (AI contribution) employs intermediate asset state representations to derive optimal portfolio allocations via a self-supervised clipped-objective policy-learner, ensuring both effectiveness and computational efficiency. Extensive evaluations on three major index datasets from China's A-share market demonstrate that SCP's superior performance in balancing risk-return trade-offs compared to state-of-the-art baselines. Exploratory and ablation studies further validate the contributions of SCP's key components.
authors: Zongshen Mu

title: Online Identification Can Replace a Floor-Plan Prior on Unseen Buildings
summary: arXiv:2611.33656v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: The Smart Buildings Challenge asks for one HVAC control policy that runs office buildings and weather it has never seen, from the building's metadata and sensor streams alone. Our controller sees no data from the target building before it runs and is not tuned per building; its few global constants were set on development scenarios. Each zone has a first-order grey-box model that starts from coefficients computed from the floor plan and is updated online by recursive least squares, and a planner and a closed-form mapping turn the models into plant commands. On two sets of buildings and weather that we generated, a validation set and a stress set with real-year weather, it scores 0.145 and 0.159 times the starter kit's PID baseline, and 0.095 times on a holdout built after all versions were fixed and scored once. It improves on every building, also against our two implementations of ASHRAE Guideline 36: per set it scores 0.60 to 0.71 times a basic version and 0.83 to 0.96 times one partly tuned on the public leaderboard, which wins one of 54 scenarios; with a 5 {\deg}C frost target for empty zones on both, the margin over the tuned version shrinks to 1.4% on the stress set, where one of six buildings is 0.2% worse. In an ablation on a reduced-order model, removing both the floor-plan prior and online identification costs 28%, 20% and 42% on the validation, stress and holdout sets, far more than the two effects combined: either source of building-specific information recovers most of what is lost without both. On one office floor in a second simulator, BOPTEST, this does not carry over: with identification on, the two priors give similar results, but the floor-plan prior alone, with constants fitted on the competition's simulator, is the least stable arm. These simulation results motivate testing floor-plan-initialised adaptive control in buildings that have drawings but no operating data.
authors: Elias T. -H. Shieh, Chun Fu

title: Verifiable but Not Predictable: What Sentence Embeddings Know About Propositional Decomposition
summary: arXiv:2611.33668v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Quality control for proposition decomposition by large language models (LLMs) raises two asymmetric questions. After decomposition, one can verify: given a sentence and a candidate proposition, does the proposition belong to that sentence? Before decomposition, one would like to predict: how many propositions should the sentence yield? On PropSegmEnt, a corpus of English Wikipedia sentences each segmented by three human annotators, we find that the two questions live in different representational spaces. A natural language inference (NLI) judge verifies membership with 92.8% accuracy and an area under the ROC curve (AUC) of 0.977, and its residual errors turn out to be mostly propositions that are true in document context rather than genuine entailment mistakes. Vector geometry cannot verify: cosine similarity saturates, and a sentence embedding is not a linear combination of its propositions' embeddings. For prediction, every symbolic anchor we test, namely token count, the CPIDR idea-density counter, and a Neo-Davidsonian predicate count, reduces to a length proxy once token count is controlled. A linear ridge probe on sentence embeddings is the only predictor that keeps genuine count signal: its length-partialled correlation with human counts is 0.40-0.49 with bootstrap confidence intervals (CIs) excluding zero, and it orders length-matched sentence pairs correctly 67-71% of the time against a 50% chance level, statistically matching the inter-annotator agreement ceiling. This signal survives INT8 quantization without loss, INT4 at a small cost, and Matryoshka truncation to 256 dimensions, and it works as well in a 2021 encoder as in a 2025 one. Its structured weakness is a systematic under-splitting of long sentences. We distill the protocol lessons, including a retracted pilot study, into a checklist for probing length-confounded quantities.
authors: Qingan Li, Tianxiao Wu, Xiling Cui

title: Node Differential Privacy via Node-Stable Graph Projections
summary: arXiv:2611.33672v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Node-differentially private algorithms enable learning on network-structured datasets in which records reflect interactions among individuals. They protect the privacy of each individual's information, including all their associated records. A key challenge in the design of such algorithms is to exploit the structure of realistic graphs---where most nodes have low degree---to achieve high accuracy, without compromising on the worst-case privacy guarantee. In this work we give two new tools for designing accurate, computationally efficient node-differentially private algorithms. First, we give a nearly linear time, randomized, node-stable graph projection: the projection leaves graphs of maximum degree $D$ unchanged, maps arbitrary graphs to subgraphs of maximum degree $\hat D \approx D$, and ensures that changing one node of the input graph has only a small effect on the distribution of the edges selected among the remaining vertices. Unlike prior approaches, which abstain when the input violates the degree bound, our projection acts as degree clipping: even when $D$ is set well below the true maximum degree (trading truncation bias at high-degree outliers for lower privacy noise), it retains at least as many edges as a maximal $D$-bounded subgraph. Second, for graphs with bounded edge weights, we give a deterministic nearly linear time Lipschitz extension for the total edge weight that agrees with the original sum on graphs of maximum degree $D$ yet is $D$-Lipschitz on all graphs. Finally, we show how to apply these methods to design node-private algorithms for high-dimensional vector summation and gradient descent on datasets where records are associated with graph edges, such as email threads.
authors: Ishaq Aden-Ali, Adam Sealfon, Adam Smith, Thomas Steinke, Jonathan Ullman

title: Nepali Currency Denomination Classification Using Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) and MobileNetV2: An Experimental Comparison
summary: arXiv:2611.33713v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Automated currency denomination recognition is a computer vision task with applications in cash handling, financial technology, and assistive systems. This study classifies seven Nepali currency denominations (Rs. 5, 10, 20, 50, 100, 500, and 1,000) using three configurations: a conventional convolutional neural network (CNN), MobileNetV2 with transfer learning, and MobileNetV2 with hyperparameter tuning. A compiled dataset of 16,249 images was used, comprising 10,500 training, 3,500 validation, and 2,249 independent test images. Images were resized to 128 x 128 pixels, normalized, and augmented to vary orientation, scale, illumination, and appearance. Models were evaluated using accuracy, precision, recall, F1-score, and precision-recall and ROC analysis. The hyperparameter-tuned MobileNetV2 achieved the highest validation accuracy (95\%), with precision, recall, and F1-score of 0.93, 0.91, and 0.92, but reached only 84\% accuracy on the held-out test set. MobileNetV2 with transfer learning but no additional tuning achieved 89\% test accuracy, and the conventional CNN achieved 85\%. Transfer learning therefore provided a competitive approach under the evaluated conditions, while higher validation accuracy from tuning did not yield higher test accuracy. To demonstrate practical deployment, a Flask-based web prototype using TensorFlow Lite was developed, supporting image upload and live webcam recognition with both visual and voice output. The study shows the feasibility of combining lightweight deep learning with a voice-assisted web interface for Nepali currency recognition, and highlights the need for more diverse datasets, greater robustness under uncontrolled imaging conditions, and broader real-world evaluation.
authors: Sakar Lamichhane, Sandesh Bhatta, Aayush Adhikari, Aaron Sapkota

title: Flipping the Coins: Training Physical Simulators through Hard Switches
summary: arXiv:2611.33716v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Hybrid simulators embed learnable components such as neural networks in physical solvers and train them on reference trajectories. Many scientific solvers feature hard switches, such as a tripping power line, an igniting grid cell, or depolarizing brain tissue, where the loss exhibits discrete jumps across switch flips, leaving standard automatic differentiation to capture only its smooth part. Existing training paradigms face a fundamentally challenging trade-off, as gradient-based relaxations smooth the switches and introduce bias across jumps, whereas derivative-free methods treat the solver as a black box and discard path gradients of the continuous dynamics. Here we introduce EventFlip, which flips a near-threshold switch from a stored state, replays the original solver, and measures the loss difference between the two runs, in effect a finite difference across the switch. By perturbing every threshold with small Gaussian noise, we cast each switch as a stochastic binary decision and derive an unbiased gradient estimator that combines the continuous path gradient with a jump term constructed from these counterfactual rollouts. EventFlip-Rand optimizes this noise-averaged objective, whereas EventFlip-Hard operates on the deterministic hard-switch simulator used at deployment and provably targets the complete discontinuous loss. Under an identical forward evaluation budget, we benchmark EventFlip against twelve baselines across a power-grid cascade, a detonation wave, and cortical spreading depolarization, achieving the lowest error on every task and reducing the strongest baseline's error by factors of 1.5, 1.4, and 1.4, respectively.
authors: Tianrun Gao, Ruiqi Feng, Haomin Wen, Tailin Wu, Liangqiong Qu, Xiaomeng Huang, Ruiqi Shu

title: Understanding Mode Collapse in Diffusion Models under Classifier-Free Guidance
summary: arXiv:2611.33719v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The use of classifier-free guidance in diffusion and flow models has proven critical to their empirical success, as it allows for the controllable generation of lower-temperature and higher-fidelity samples. Despite its widespread use, classifier-free guidance remains both empirically and theoretically poorly understood, owing to the difficulty of solving the associated transport equations for arbitrary normalizing flows. In this paper, we observe that the effects of classifier-free guidance arise from a mismatch between the representation capabilities of the conditional and unconditional distributions, wherein the conditional distribution exhibits higher complexity and fidelity. We propose an analytical model to capture this observation: the conditional distribution is a Gaussian mixture whose means lie on an ellipsoid, and the unconditional distribution is a single Gaussian approximating the mixture. The flows arising from this mixture are closed under scaling, enabling us to derive analytic closed-form solutions for the guided distribution at all noise scales and guidance levels. Our analytic solution shows that classifier-free guidance induces (a) a shift along a mean-axis direction and (b) a persistent skew toward, and concentration around, a singular point corresponding to the conditional sample starting from zero noise. We validate our theoretical predictions on pretrained, large-scale image diffusion models.
authors: Daniel Pfrommer, Chenyang Yuan, Frank Permenter, Ali Jadbabaie

title: CovNovBench: A Benchmark for Evaluating Time Series Foundation Models under Covariate Novelty
summary: arXiv:2611.33732v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Covariate-aware time-series foundation models (TSFMs) condition their forecasts on additional input variables, called covariates, that are supplied over the future horizon. This capability makes them appealing for interventional forecasting, in which a target is predicted under a planned action such as a new product pricing policy or a new patient treatment schedule. We refer to covariates that encode such actions as treatment covariates. Current covariate-aware TSFMs, however, are trained on observed patterns, and their behavior is unclear when future treatment covariates fall outside the range seen in the history. Examples include a numerical treatment that leaves its historical range and a categorical treatment that takes a previously unseen policy. We call this practically common setting covariate novelty, and note that it is not systematically represented in existing benchmarks. We introduce an operational definition of covariate novelty and use it to construct CovNovBench, a benchmark of 88,476 evaluation series generated or filtered from four simulator-based and real-world datasets. The benchmark spans categorical and numerical treatment covariates as well as stable and trending targets. We evaluate six covariate-aware TSFMs zero-shot using point and directional accuracy metrics. No model is consistently reliable in our benchmark: point error almost always increases under covariate novelty, directional performance changes non-uniformly, and the best observed model varies across datasets and metrics. CovNovBench provides a systematic testbed for developing TSFMs that forecast more reliably under covariate novelty.
authors: Wenhao Pan, Ravi Kiran Selvam, Michael W. Mahoney, Mayank Jauhari, Mengfei Cao, Dmitry Efimov, Boris N. Oreshkin

title: FlashProve-Next: Verifiable Inference for Production LLM APIs
summary: arXiv:2611.33741v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Clients of closed-weight LLM APIs cannot verify whether a provider ran the advertised model, precision, hidden prompt, and reasoning budget. Existing approaches either trust hardware or third parties, or re-prove every layer of an integer surrogate at high cost while diverging from native floating-point serving. FlashProve-Next produces verifiable, zero-knowledge-masked proofs for individual LLM API responses without modifying native serving (bf16/fp8/mxfp4, random sampling, FlashAttention, CUDA graphs, batching, prefix caching) and without disclosing weights, hidden prompts, hidden reasoning, or activations (dense profiles fix coarse geometry; cross-architecture hiding is deferred). A non-depleting Reed-Solomon weight commitment model_id opens inside proofs via hidden column openings, while local per-operator rounding contracts remove integer surrogates and the refusal-bit leak. Cost-weighted spot-checking supports non-interactive public verification (NI-315, $\varepsilon \le 2^{-40}$, $Q \le 2^{64}$) and external-seed C_pre mode (ExtSeed-153, $\varepsilon \le 2^{-20}$, $Q_{\rm samp} \le 2^{30}$). Twenty-eight Lean 4 modules (696 declarations, zero sorry, standard axioms only) mechanize round-by-round soundness, bucketed sampling, $\mathbb{F}_{p^3}$ constrained-mask binding, causal masking, six IR gadgets, and executable FPN2 verifiers. Five-model Blackwell calibration gives zero false rejections across 1.85M GEMM/MoE blocks and 1.96M non-GEMM rows. Our zero-Phase-2 folded backend (folded ZK simulator open) proves Qwen3-0.6B ExtSeed-153 (1.47B cells, 8 MiB) in 450.2 s GPU (10.76 s CPU) at unique-decoding $Q=128$, passes a 14/14 cheating matrix, and scales to 36-layer Qwen3-4B (dev $4+2$) and live vLLM Qwen3-30B-A3B-FP8 Relation 6 (1.49 s prove, 23.4 ms Rust verify, public weight tiles). Rust fpn-verify checks 8 MiB FPN2 Relation 2 proofs in 10.1 ms on CPU.
authors: Liang Song

title: OrbACE: Orbital and Atomic Cluster Expansion
summary: arXiv:2611.33743v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Accurate electronic-structure reference data are expensive, motivating interatomic potentials that learn effectively from limited training sets. We introduce OrbACE (Orbital and Atomic Cluster Expansion), a framework that supplements an E(3)-equivariant cluster-expansion backbone with inexpensive electronic-structure descriptors. On ANI-1x at the $\omega$B97X/6-31G* level, its atom-centered variant, OrbACE-A, trained on 10,000 configurations and evaluated on 442,000 held-out configurations, achieves energy and force mean absolute errors of 3.16 meV/atom and 76 meV/angstrom in direct learning, compared with 9.61 meV/atom and 146 meV/angstrom for MACE with matched backbone settings. This reduces the energy error by a factor of three and approximately halves the force error. Its energy error is also below that of the best delta-corrected MACE baseline, 5.00 meV/atom, although its force error is slightly higher. Combining OrbACE-A with a Hartree-Fock delta baseline further reduces the errors to 1.48 meV/atom and 35 meV/angstrom. OrbACE-A builds atom- and pair-resolved invariants from a non-self-consistent extended-Hueckel model evaluated within the differentiable forward pass, yielding forces consistent with the predicted energy. The orbital variant, OrbACE-O, instead uses localized Hartree-Fock orbitals as graph nodes, with scalar and equivariant electronic descriptors. Its forces are evaluated at fixed descriptors, omitting their response to nuclear motion. In direct learning on ANI-1x, its energy error is approximately three times that of OrbACE-A. The three benchmarks considered (ANI-1x, revised MD17, and 3BPA) cover neutral, closed-shell, non-periodic molecules containing H, C, N, and O. Performance outside this domain remains to be established.
authors: Etinosa Osaro, Dario Rocca

title: Understanding Double Descent through Universal Compression
summary: arXiv:2611.33759v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Many deep learning models exhibit a double-descent phenomenon, where test loss exhibits a sharp peak near the interpolation threshold and then descends a second time as model size grows further, contrary to the U-shape predicted by the classical bias--variance tradeoff. The double-descent phenomenon has been found and explained in toy classical models, but is not well-understood in modern deep learning despite extensive empirical study. We interpret double descent through the novel lens of universal compression. Specifically, we upper bound the maximum-likelihood excess test loss as a sum of four terms: an approximation-and-shift term, a minimax batch regret, a prior cost, and an MLE-vs-Bayes gap. Under exact posterior sampling, we further show that the expected MLE-vs-ensemble gap lower-bounds the MLE-vs-Bayes gap in the well-specified setting. In our experiments, a Gaussian-prior SGLD approximation to the Bayes predictor, unlike SGD, shows no pronounced interpolation peak. Experiments with uniform random labels support this gap as a major contributor to the double-descent peak; here, the SGD cross-entropy is roughly four times the SGLD ensemble cross-entropy at the peak, while the ensemble cross-entropy remains near $\log 10$.
authors: Jiaxuan Cheng, Addison Spiegel

title: Don't Waste the Population: Post-Anneal Refinement for Combinatorial Optimization
summary: arXiv:2611.33766v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Parallel annealers generate diverse candidate solutions; yet, conventional post-processing typically refines only the best, leaving much of the population's potential untapped. We introduce Iterative Path-Relinking Polish (I-PRP), a deterministic, training-free method that exploits this diversity to discover better solutions without modifying the underlying annealing process. I-PRP selects promising candidates, explores cost-guided paths between locally optimized solutions, and refines intermediate states to uncover better local minima. Newly discovered improvements are iteratively incorporated into the population, enabling further exploration. We theoretically guarantee that I-PRP never degrades solution quality relative to conventional single-candidate polishing on the same population and converges in finitely many iterations. Experiments across challenging combinatorial optimization benchmarks, including MaxCut, MaxClique, and graph coloring, demonstrate substantial improvements in several instances. Paired evaluations confirm non-degradation, while matched-runtime comparisons show that exploiting existing population diversity can outperform additional annealing. These results establish I-PRP as an effective and reliable refinement strategy for parallel annealing.
authors: Yuma Ichikawa

title: RHOPE: LLM-Augmented Adaptive Experimental Design with Complex Contextual Information
summary: arXiv:2611.33767v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Experimental design allocates limited measurement effort across candidate treatments to learn their expected outcomes. Adaptive designs refine allocations as evidence accumulates, improving estimation and treatment selection. Contextual information can inform these decisions, but exploiting unstructured or high-dimensional context remains challenging. We use large language models (LLMs) to transform complex context into proxy outcomes and propose Residual Horizon Optimization for Prediction-Powered Experimentation (RHOPE), a principled Bayesian adaptive experimentation framework that combines true outcomes with LLM-generated proxy outcomes and formulates finite-batch design as a posterior Markov decision process (MDP). Our methodology uses proxy outcomes in two ways: sample augmentation improves estimation precision, while observing proxies before each allocation decision provides advance information. Synthetic experiments and semi-synthetic experiments using Genomics of Drug Sensitivity in Cancer (GDSC) data suggest that estimation precision drives most gains, with smaller advance-information gains, and highlight the importance of proxy informativeness and moment-estimation accuracy.
authors: Bowen Shi, Bo Li

title: Robust Adaptive Channel Estimation for RIS-Assisted mmWave Massive MIMO via a Stochastic Shannon Entropy Criterion
summary: arXiv:2611.33773v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Accurate channel estimation in reconfigurable intelligent surface (RIS)-assisted millimeter-wave (mmWave) massive multiple-input multiple-output (MIMO) systems remains challenging due to the passive nature of the RIS, the high dimensionality of the cascaded channel, and the presence of non-Gaussian impulsive disturbances. This paper proposes a robust sparsity-aware adaptive estimator, termed reweighted zero-attracting stochastic Shannon entropy (RZA-SSE), for angular-domain channel estimation. The algorithm combines a double-window kernel-based Shannon entropy criterion with a norm-normalized \(\ell_1\) penalty. Both the data-driven term and the nonsmooth penalty are differentiated using exact Wirtinger calculus. An exact weight-error recursion and a mean-square energy relation are derived. Local stability is analyzed via a joint coefficient--penalty state representation, and an approximate steady-state mean-square deviation (MSD) expression is obtained. Extensive simulations under Gaussian-mixture impulsive noise demonstrate that ZA-SSE consistently outperforms the state-of-the-art benchmarks in steady-state MSD.
authors: Mojtaba Hajiabadi, Saeid Pakravan, Hadi Zayyani, Mohammad Salman, Ming Zeng

title: InterGenEHR$^+$: An Interactive Framework for Natural Language-Conditioned Generation of Longitudinal Patient Trajectories
summary: arXiv:2611.33788v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Objective: To develop and validate InterGenEHR$^+$, an interactive framework for natural language-conditioned generation of synthetic tabular electronic health records (EHRs) and longitudinal trajectories for scenario-based evaluation of machine learning models. Methods: An optional large language model (LLM) parser converts clinical requests into structured constraints. Conditional variational autoencoders and diffusion models generate single-time-point records, while diffusion models generate longitudinal trajectories. We evaluate parsing, distributional fidelity, imputation, clinical-constraint adherence, mortality prediction, and clinical plausibility using a multi-institutional cohort of 874 patients receiving venovenous extracorporeal membrane oxygenation (VV-ECMO). Results: Gemma 3 4B with few-shot prompting achieves the highest parsing performance with a low spurious slot rate. IGE-TabDDPM and IGE-PMVAE perform well in single-time-point generation; IGE-CSDI, IGE-FGTI, and IGE-MTSCI lead on different longitudinal fidelity metrics. Across five random seeds and three classifiers, synthetic cohorts retain predictive utility for mortality prediction on real test data. Clinician ratings support trajectory plausibility and alignment with requested scenarios. Conclusion: InterGenEHR$^+$ supports clinician-specified generation of EHR trajectories with statistical fidelity and downstream predictive utility in the evaluated VV-ECMO cohort. Extension to other clinical settings requires further validation. Significance: The framework supports scenario-based evaluation of machine learning models in data-sparse critical care settings.
authors: Yu Yang, Jiafeng Song, Baraa F Abed, Christina Creel, Sagar B Dave, Henry Foote, Lisa Lima, Victor Moas, Craig S Jabaley, Rishikesan Kamaleswaran, Pan Xu

title: QPAT: A Universal Quantum Machine Learning Framework for Quantum-Assisted Training and Classical Inference
summary: arXiv:2611.33806v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Deep learning models often struggle with sharp local optima and overfitting in limited-data regimes, and exhibit limited capacity for capturing high-order, complex probability distributions. Quantum Machine Learning (QML) models, by operating in exponentially large Hilbert spaces, can efficiently represent such distributions and provide favorable inductive biases for learning, offering a promising pathway to overcome these limitations. However, their practical deployment in the Noisy Intermediate-Scale Quantum (NISQ) era is severely hindered by gradient coupling, barren plateaus, data-loading bottlenecks, and high inference latency. To bridge classical AI and QML, we propose QPAT (QCBM-Prior-Assisted Training), a universal framework that employs a Quantum Circuit Born Machine (QCBM) as a learnable generative prior to provide a task-aligned structured inductive bias during classical model training. The framework can be seamlessly integrated into any classical backbone, including LSTMs, CNNs, and Transformers. We introduce a decoupled fitness-based scoring mechanism and a stochastic "Drop-Prior" mechanism to implicitly distill quantum structural knowledge into the classical weights during training. Evaluated extensively on six benchmarks spanning time-series forecasting, computer vision, and natural language processing, our framework consistently outperforms purely classical backbones in both predictive performance and stability across random seeds; ablation studies further show that these gains are not reproduced by unstructured random priors or a classically learned generative prior. Remarkably, our approach enables completely classical inference, bypassing quantum latency while preserving quantum-enhanced accuracy, paving a highly practical path for QML deployment.
authors: Yixiong Chen

title: KnitNet: Learning to Search at Inference Time for Exact RNA Inverse Design
summary: arXiv:2611.33812v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: RNA inverse design seeks nucleotide sequences that fold into specified target structures. Existing methods rely on learned generators that can miss exact structural matches, especially beyond their training distributions, or on costly search over a vast, multimodal sequence space. Search is further complicated by globally coupled nucleotide interactions, as correcting one pairing error can create new errors beyond a fixed repair scope. To address this, we introduce KnitNet, an inference-time scaling framework that learns from verifier feedback to refine sequences for exact fold-back matching. Starting from candidates generated for a target secondary structure, KnitNet uses mismatched folds to infer nucleotide dependencies and adapt its joint repair strategy, while an online surrogate learns to predict which edits are promising. This makes search progressively more informed and compute-efficient. Crucially, KnitNet generalizes across RNA structural regimes by changing only the optimization signal to match the verifier required by each setting. Across five secondary-structure benchmarks, KnitNet increases exact solve rates by an average of 21 percentage points over continued sampling with 70% less time-to-solve. On OpenKnot57 specifically, KnitNet is the first method to achieve exact computational matches for all complex, pseudoknotted structures. Beyond 2D, KnitNet improves 3D structural self-consistency over per-target RL by 7.8% while being 39.3% faster, demonstrating generalization and effective inference-time scaling across RNA design regimes.
authors: Antonia Panescu, Xin Wang, Haoran Xu, Qingyu Chen, Carlos Oliver, Rex Ying

title: MetaDecomp: Adaptive Task Decomposition via Meta-Learned Procedural Memory
summary: arXiv:2611.33822v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Reusing past experience in long-horizon tasks requires more than storing successful procedures: Language agents must distinguish which procedures apply and what work remains as execution progresses. We introduce MetaDecomp, an in-context meta-learning framework for adaptive task decomposition that jointly learns a task-relative state space and reusable procedures. Its outer loop builds procedural memory from successful training executions, representing task progress as abstract states and procedures between states as directed acyclic graphs of operations and dependencies. As new progress distinctions are learned, MetaDecomp revisits historical execution evidence to reassess state assignments and reorganize the procedures they support. With memory fixed at test time, the inner loop refines an initial decomposition and revises it from environmental feedback, combining applicable procedure fragments with task-specific steps missing from memory. Evaluated on ALFWorld and ScienceWorld over three seeds, MetaDecomp achieves the highest mean performance among the compared methods in four of five settings, for example, an 86.3% success rate on ALFWorld with Qwen3-4B. Fixing the initial schema or omitting historical reprojection reduces performance in component ablations. MetaDecomp also uses fewer inference tokens than ReAct and AutoRefine in all five settings. Cross-benchmark analysis identifies a low-performance area where partial coverage degrades success relative to hidden memory; high coverage improves success, while low coverage changes little. Code will be released upon acceptance.
authors: Ziyi Wang, Yixiao He, Yichen Wu, Ruite Lu, Jiayu Wang, Ying Wei

title: Pitfalls of Dependency-Ready Decoding for Masked Diffusion Language Models
summary: arXiv:2611.33823v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Masked diffusion models (MDMs) have shown strong performance on structured reasoning tasks such as Sudoku, Trip Planning, and Countdown. MDMs introduce a freedom in the order in which tokens may be unmasked, and to exercise this freedom for good accuracy, early decoding strategies relied on signals of confidence or the downstream impact of decoding a token. However, simple examples seem to illustrate that resolving a token's dependencies before unmasking it should be important. Therefore, we examine whether this principle, which we call dependency-ready decoding, would contribute to better accuracy, from a practical and a theoretical perspective. We examine a recent decoder that implements dependency-readiness through attention, and generally find that when it performs better than confidence-based or future utility baselines, its decoding order collapses to left-to-right decoding. For theoretical analysis, we establish a definition of dependency without resorting to attention, measured by an information-theoretic score of how much revealing a single masked token (or a set) would shift the model's prediction for another. We prove that when the margin is large relative to this score, no such revelation can change the top prediction, so in this regime Maximum-Margin decoding already commits dependency-ready tokens. These findings leave only a narrow scope for future dependency-ready decoders: their potential benefit is limited to positions with margins smaller than the information-theoretic sensitivity, and reliance on attention should be questioned.
authors: Lina Berrayana, Christopher Malon, Yoichi Ishibashi, Taichi Aida, Masafumi Oyamada

title: On Grokking and the Dynamics of Generalization
summary: arXiv:2611.33825v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We extend the signal-channel theory of grokking introduced by Litman and Guo by relating training dissipation and evaluation transfer to population risk. For preconditioned gradient flows with time-dependent kernels, we distinguish two sources of limited evaluation visibility, namely small cumulative dissipation and weak transfer. We obtain quantitative bounds for task visibility and establish their stability under signal filtering and changes of evaluation distribution. We describe how task directions enter the effective signal channel through spectral activation or transport. We establish necessary and sufficient conditions for the transferred signal to decrease squared population risk and derive classification error bounds under margin assumptions. These results yield sufficient conditions for the same training trajectory to generalize under one evaluation distribution while failing under another. We show that differences in spectral learning rates can produce arbitrarily long delays between low training loss and low population risk. By relating classification accuracy to the distribution of margin crossing times, we construct a family of gradient flows in which the generalization delay tends to infinity, while both the duration of the transition from zero to full accuracy and the corresponding variation of population risk tend to zero. These phenomena occur without feature evolution during training. Finally, we prove that the occurrence and timing of generalization cannot generally be inferred from training dynamics alone, but depend on the geometry of evaluation transfer and its relation to the target.
authors: Malik Amir

title: FEAST: Fair and Efficient Adaptive Sampling for Task-Free On-Policy Learning
summary: arXiv:2611.33827v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Language agents trained from self-generated experience must allocate a limited rollout budget across heterogeneous capabilities. A common strategy is to prioritize capabilities with strong current learning signals, but in on-policy learning these signals are endogenous: past allocation changes the policy and therefore the evidence available for future allocation. This can create a feedback loop in which under-trained capabilities receive increasingly fewer opportunities to improve. We formalize this effect through the Quota-Efficiency Law (QEL), which shows that allocation history can change learning efficiency even under matched capability-specific exposure. Motivated by this, we introduce FEAST, a task-free adaptive sampling framework that separates opportunity allocation from compute allocation. FEAST dynamically discovers capability clusters while preserving their learning histories, maintains continued sampling opportunities across clusters, and reserves a rollout budget for each selected cluster. Within each budget, it progressively concentrates computation on prompts with informative reward variation. Across GURU-18K and SMC, FEAST improves average performance over competitive adaptive sampling baselines under matched rollout budgets, while better preserving learning progress on weaker capabilities. Ablation studies further support the complementary roles of cross-cluster opportunity protection and within-cluster selective allocation. Code will be released upon acceptance.
authors: Yongxi Zhu, Ziyi Wang, Yichen Wu, Ruite Lu, Liao Chang, Haipeng Li, Ying Wei

title: Learning a Whole-Body Pivot-Walking Gait for Heavy-Box Transport with a Humanoid
summary: arXiv:2611.33828v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Through pivot walking, humans can transport objects that are too heavy to lift. Previous humanoid studies have relied on planned sequences in which object manipulation and stepping are executed separately and the object is brought to rest between successive rotations. However, few studies have developed a single learned controller for humanoid pivot walking. In this paper, we propose a single reinforcement-learning policy that jointly coordinates stepping, balance control, and object manipulation. The policy is trained using rewards that promote alternating pivot motions and a phase reference that progresses according to the displacement of the object. In simulation, we confirmed that the humanoid can pivot a box. For deployment, we fine-tuned the policy into an object-blind version that follows a periodic clock instead of the progress reference. On the real robot, the deployed policy transported the box forward by more than 1 m in all five trials; each trial ended at a base-tilt safety stop. These results demonstrate that coordinated humanoid pivot walking can be learned with reinforcement learning and transferred to a physical humanoid robot without direct object-state sensing.
authors: Rikuto Hidaka, Tsung-Yuan Chen, Kento Kawaharazuka

title: VoroPlex: A Python Framework for Multi-Threaded and Differentiable Voronoi Tessellation
summary: arXiv:2611.33829v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Voronoi tessellations are widely used in computational physics, for example to measure local structure in particle systems and to generate meshes. We present VoroPlex, an open-source Python package for computing Voronoi tessellations in two and three dimensions. VoroPlex is built on the multi-threaded version of the C++ library Voro++, so that large tessellations can be computed in parallel. The package also makes the tessellation differentiable. Each Voronoi vertex is labeled by the generators that define it, and VoroPlex uses these labels to compute the derivative of the vertex with respect to the positions of these generators. PyTorch can therefore compute gradients of quantities such as cell areas, volumes, and interface areas with respect to the generator positions, so that these quantities can be optimized using standard gradient-based methods. The package also includes tools for extracting interfaces between groups of cells and for exporting meshes. For one million points using 28 threads, VoroPlex is 46 times faster than SciPy in 2D and 39 times faster in 3D. We demonstrate the package with three applications: centroidal Voronoi tessellations with a variable density, meshing of 2D shapes defined by signed distance functions, and the design of foams with a preferred cell orientation.
authors: Peihang Lin, Shanmei Wanyan, Mucheng Zhu, Ying Jiang, Chris H. Rycroft, Chenfanfu Jiang, Jiayin Lu

title: The Missing Root: Geometric Imagination Without Images in Large Language Models
summary: arXiv:2611.33841v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: This paper proposes a new paradigm and method for giving large language models spatial understanding. Standard language models operate exclusively over discrete words (secondary representations of things rather than continuous space itself), forcing them to guess geometry verbally. Whereas most multimodal approaches equate spatial grounding with camera images or video frames, spatial structure itself is not a picture: it consists of coordinate frames, solid boundaries, and how objects move and relate to each other in continuous space. Motivated by this distinction, we place continuous object tokens combining pose (position, orientation, and scale) and signed-distance shape embeddings alongside word tokens inside a single uninterrupted transformer sequence, allowing language and geometry to attend to each other as object scenes are built and updated step by step. Control tokens switch output automatically between natural-language words and continuous object state updates to a persistent object workspace, while an attention mask blocks earlier prose when generating the answer, so responses must be read directly from settled geometry. To prove this method works, we attach a narrow parallel spatial stream (+4.4% weights) alongside unfrozen Qwen3-1.7B layers. In our two-dimensional tests, the model spawns and transforms multi-object scenes from English descriptions, transfers shapes to held-out nouns, and relies causally on the workspace to answer spatial questions.
authors: Lo\"ic Magnan, Tomasz Kozlowski

title: ChemDeduce: Benchmarking LLMs for Unknown Chemical Identification through Interactive Simulated Experiments
summary: arXiv:2611.33848v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have shown strong performance in chemical knowledge and reasoning, yet it remains unclear whether they can solve problems whose answers must be discovered through experimentation. We investigate this question through Unknown Chemical Identification, where a model must actively design experiments, interpret observations, update hypotheses, and ultimately identify a hidden substance. We introduce ChemDeduce, an interactive evaluation framework for assessing LLMs through simulated experiments. ChemDeduce formulates chemical identification as a sequential decision process and provides a stateful simulated laboratory with explicit instrument and operational constraints, enabling scalable and reproducible evaluation of iterative experimental reasoning. We benchmark eight frontier LLMs on 200 chemicals, yielding 1600 model--target pairs and 4800 episodes over three independent repetitions, and evaluate identification accuracy, operational compliance, interaction efficiency, and trajectory-level reasoning quality. Despite generating seemingly plausible experimental plans, current models achieve an average identification accuracy ranging from 23.83% to 67.33%, revealing substantial limitations in experiment selection, evidence interpretation, and sequential hypothesis refinement.
authors: Hengyi Cai, Yuqi Tang, Zichang Li, Huajun chen, Qiang Zhang, Keyan Ding

title: Mitigating Overgeneralization in RND via Spectral Target Design
summary: arXiv:2611.33850v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Random Network Distillation (RND) is a scalable novelty signal for RL based on a fixed random target network and a trained predictor. However, it can overgeneralize: the predictor extrapolates the random target off the data manifold, causing novelty scores to collapse on unfamiliar inputs. This paper analyzes this failure through a kernel-theoretic lens. Under a GP target model and an NTK-regime predictor, we show that the RND novelty score is a cross-kernel residual variance: it is governed jointly by the target covariance kernel and the predictor NTK, rather than by either one alone. This identifies overgeneralization as spectral under-excitation. Motivated by this view, we formulate spectral target design as a principle for shaping RND novelty geometry. As a concrete instance, we replace the implicit random-network target with a bandwidth-controlled Random Fourier Feature (RFF) target, redistributing residual signal toward modes less attenuated by the predictor. Experiments on offline D4RL, online Atari, and Fetch manipulation benchmarks show improved novelty discrimination and downstream RL performance. The code for the RL implementation is available at https://github.com/tuuktuc86/RFF-RND.
authors: Minseok Jeong, Yechan Lee, Hyewon Choi, Jeongyong Yang, SooJean Han

title: Normalizing Flows are Capable World Models
summary: arXiv:2611.33872v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: A world model lets an agent anticipate the consequences of its actions and use imagined futures to make decisions. We introduce Normalizing-Flow World Model (NFWM), which pairs an invertible observation encoder with an action-conditioned probabilistic predictor. Because the encoder is invertible, the predicted distribution over latent states defines a distribution over future observations. Maximizing the exact conditional likelihood of those observations therefore trains the representation and dynamics jointly. An agent can plan directly in the learned latent space and decode sampled trajectories to inspect possible futures. On Teleport, these samples capture the two possible outcomes of the same action. In Flappy Bird, a world model trained by likelihood alone supports reward-based planning that reaches 100 pipes in all ten evaluated games. For goal-conditioned control, an auxiliary inverse-dynamics objective shapes the coordinates used to compare predicted states with a goal. On LIBERO, NFWM uses this distance to select successful action sequences more often than LeWM and SMWM. In Atari Boxing, training on imagined trajectories improves a policy beyond its behavior-cloned initialization. Together, these results establish normalizing flows as capable world models.
authors: Zijia Li, Yong-Hyun Park, Shusheng Yang, Jiatao Gu

title: Random Voronoi Networks
summary: arXiv:2611.33875v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Nearest-neighbor methods are local, simple, and interpretable, but their non-parametric form makes them memory-intensive, expensive at inference, and difficult to integrate into differentiable neural architectures. We introduce Random Voronoi Networks (RVNs), a family of structured three-layer MLPs that express nearest-neighbor geometry through sampled Voronoi comparisons. The first layer computes Random Voronoi Features (RVF) from affine pairwise separators between selected training samples, the second layer aggregates these comparisons into Voronoi cells or top-k neighborhood scores, and the readout layer produces classification or regression predictions. We show that, when all samples and pairwise comparisons are included, step RVNs recover exact Euclidean k-NN, while ReLU RVNs provide a violation-score realization for 1-NN that can be relaxed into a differentiable soft weighting. Subsampling yields approximate RVNs with explicit control over the number of cells and features. We study several unsupervised sampling methods that trade off random coverage, directional diversity, coordinate sparsity, and empirical feature variance. Empirically, RVFs produce a highly effective data encoding strategy, providing performance boosts to downstream methods ranging from linear to modern tabular deep learning models. Finally, we showcase that RVF provides an interpretable feature map due to its k-NN based construction and ties to pairwise local directions. These results position our Random Voronoi formulation as a bridge between nearest-neighbor rules, random features, and modern tabular models.
authors: Ray Verma, Pau Mateo-Bernard\'o, Daniel Mas Montserrat, David Bonet, Mar\c{c}al Comajoan Cara, Alexander G. Ioannidis

title: The Gradient Difference Induced by Detaching the Denominator in QK Normalization
summary: arXiv:2611.33887v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: QK normalization divides each query and key by its own RMS norm before the attention scores are computed. Treating this denominator as a constant during backpropagation leaves the forward pass unchanged but alters the parameter gradients. We derive a closed form for the difference between the gradient under this detached rule and the gradient under the standard rule. For a single token, this difference is parallel to the token's own query; it changes only the query norm and has no first-order effect after normalization. The queries, however, are computed by a projection matrix $W_Q$ shared across all tokens. The gradient difference on $W_Q$ therefore equals $W_Q$ right-multiplied by a weighted second moment of the inputs, and it decomposes exactly into three components: a radial component that changes only the norm of $W_Q$, a tangential component that changes the query directions of other tokens, and an upstream component that changes the gradient passed to earlier layers. Under AdamW, the radial component drives $W_Q$ to a larger equilibrium norm and reduces its angular update per step. Paired experiments on a small Transformer language model are consistent with this analysis. Detaching the query denominator consistently raises the test loss, and the gap persists across hardware, evaluation datasets and learning rates. All three components remain non-negligible throughout training, with the tangential component the largest. Norm growth and the smaller angular update appear only on the detached projection matrix, while the other projection matrix is essentially unchanged. With a learnable scale, however, we observe no resolvable loss gap.
authors: Yuanqi Zhang, Haocheng Wang, Congping Lin

title: On the Learnability of Model Reprogramming: A Reachability and Relabeling Perspective
summary: arXiv:2611.33889v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Model reprogramming adapts a frozen source model to a target task by wrapping it in a learnable input transformation from target input to the source-model input space, and an output mapping from source-model outputs to target predictions. Despite extensive empirical progress, the finite-sample learnability of the induced wrapper hypothesis class $\mathcal{F}_{\rm MR}$ remains underexplored. We address this for source models that expose hard source labels and analyze it through the wrapper structure: on any target samples, the input transformation selects reachable source labels that the output mapping relabels. Through this lens, we answer two questions: (1) how many target samples are needed to approach the best predictor in $\mathcal{F}_{\rm MR}$, and (2) what gap remains between the optimum over $\mathcal{F}_{\rm MR}$ and the target Bayes risk. For (1), the wrapper structure factorizes the sample-wise complexity of $\mathcal{F}_{\rm MR}$ into a reachability term counting reachable source-label patterns, and a conditional relabeling term counting their relabelings. This yields an agnostic-PAC bound on the estimation error, with sample complexity scaling additively in the two terms; this bound becomes closed-form on additive input transformations and is matched by a lower bound on an explicit binary classification construction. For (2), the same structure decomposes the approximation error exactly into the source-label information loss and output-mapping restriction with a source-conditional upper bound on this gap. We extend the approximation analysis to logit-exposing source models, where the upper bound is empirically estimable. The wrapper-side analysis localizes both errors to specific components, giving a structural view of reprogramming practice.
authors: Zesheneg Ye, Pin-Yu Chen, Feng Liu

title: Looped Models are Fast Multi-Token Predictors
summary: arXiv:2611.33896v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Looped language models can adapt computation for predicting a token without a proportional rescaling in unique model parameters by adjusting the number of loops. This property has been used for self-speculative decoding, taking shallow loops as fast drafters and deep loops as verifiers, which is effective since drafting still uses full parameters. In this paper, we show that shallow loops can be also predictive of several future tokens and leverage this to drastically accelerate the inference of looped language models. To that end, we present Floodgates, a simple self-speculative decoding method that appends a block of mask tokens as a suffix and learns via low-rank adaptation to draft these tokens in parallel. Across seven models, five benchmarks, a range of batch sizes, and both greedy and sampled decoding, Floodgates is the fastest lossless decoding method in most cases, attaining up to 7.5x acceleration. Through analysis, we show that this speedup is enabled by all-depth training of looped models, with the shallow drafter's ability to leverage full-depth computation by conditioning on deep prefix cache evaluated during verification.
authors: Ayhan Suleymanzade, Sean McLeish, Sehoon Kim, Jinwoo Kim, Antoine Bosselut

title: Correlation-Aware Evidential Fusion for Trusted Multi-View Classification
summary: arXiv:2611.33900v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Trusted multi-view classification aims to make accurate and reliable predictions by integrating information from multiple views. Existing methods typically estimate class evidence and uncertainty for each view and combine the resulting opinions through aggregation rules. However, they generally treat different views as independent information sources, overlooking the correlations among them. Highly correlated views tend to produce similar evidence, and treating them as independent sources may repeatedly count consistent information and give it disproportionate influence, while weakening complementary evidence that provides additional information. Consequently, such correlation-unaware fusion may not only limit classification performance but also produce miscalibrated uncertainty estimates. To address this issue, we propose Correlation-Aware Fusion of Evidence (CAFE), a framework for trusted multi-view classification. CAFE applies complementarity-based trust discounting to the evidence produced by view-private experts and introduces a correlation-aware constraint to reduce the repeated contribution of similar evidence. It then learns sample-specific weights from the global multi-view context to adaptively combine the correlation-adjusted private evidence with cross-view collaborative evidence. Extensive experiments on six real-world datasets demonstrate that CAFE consistently improves classification and calibration performance in general settings, with particularly significant gains when strong correlations exist among views.
authors: Tianyang Wang, Mengchi Zuo, Cai Xu, Yilin Zhang, Ziyu Guan, Wei Zhao

title: InstructTTS-OPD: On-Policy Distillation for Multi-Objective Instruction-Following TTS
summary: arXiv:2611.33937v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Instruction-following text-to-speech (Instruct-TTS) renders a target transcript in the manner described by a free-form natural-language instruction, and a good rendition must succeed on three fronts at once: following the instruction, pronouncing the transcript correctly, and sounding natural. Reinforcement learning has become the standard way to post-train such generative models toward human preferences, and TTS systems increasingly adopt it. When the three objectives are optimized together under a single scalar reward, typically with group relative policy optimization (GRPO), training tends to be unstable: the objectives compete, and the shared update drifts toward whichever one is easiest to improve, producing a seesaw among them. We instead adapt on-policy distillation (OPD), which fuses several single-objective teachers by matching their velocity fields on the student's own rollouts. Realizing this for Instruct-TTS first calls for a sound reward on each axis, which we analyze carefully: a distilled Qwen-Omni proxy for the costly Gemini judge, dialect-free data for the WER reward, and DNSMOS in place of the language-biased UTMOS. We then train three single-objective teachers with GRPO and fuse them with OPD, routing each rollout to the instruction-following or WER teacher by its data domain and letting every rollout additionally follow the MOS teacher for quality. This lets instruction following and intelligibility improve together without a trade-off, but the quality target conflicts with instruction following, so following it additively reintroduces the seesaw. We therefore propose conflict-aware velocity fusion, which projects the quality target off the direction that opposes the primary objective before fusing, and show that it markedly reduces the instruction-following/quality trade-off. The fused model improves over scalar-reward GRPO on all three objectives at once.
authors: Haitao Li, Tian Tan, Yuguang Yang, Guanrou Yang, Wenhao Guan, Chenglin Li, Shan Yang, Xie Chen

title: CondUQ: Calibrated Conditional Uncertainty Quantification Using Distribution Matching
summary: arXiv:2611.33939v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Many applications, especially reliability- and safety-critical ones, require accurate uncertainty quantification for the outputs of model- or learning-based measurement, estimation, and prediction systems. The errors of such systems often vary with factors such as input quality and operating conditions, and thus cannot be accurately described by a single Gaussian model. Although Gaussian mixture models and calibrated quantiles can approximate such error distributions, their unconditional forms do not capture how the error behavior depends on these factors. Hence, we propose condUQ, an approach that conditions error models on observable factors for enabling accurate and reliable uncertainty quantification. condUQ is built on top of an existing system without modifying it and applies even when the system is a black box. First, condUQ maps the observable factors to a latent quality index (QI) such that errors sharing the same QI follow a common, approximately Gaussian conditional distribution. The QI predictor is trained end-to-end with a distribution-matching objective, without requiring quality labels. Second, for each QI, a Gaussian error model is then fitted and calibrated on a large held-out dataset. condUQ is demonstrated on three examples: (a) GPS multipath errors conditioned on satellite elevation and signal strength, (b) relative attitude errors of a transformer-based visual relative pose regression model conditioned on its internal features of the image pairs, and (c) prediction errors of a world model conditioned on the input observations and actions. In all three examples, condUQ substantially reduces the discrepancy between the modeled and empirical error distributions compared with a single global model. Moreover, the learned QIs reveal how the underlying factors affect the error characteristics in a manner consistent with physical principles.
authors: Shizhuang Wang, Tianhao Wang, Xingqun Zhan

title: A Graphical Criterion for Linear Causal Bounds
summary: arXiv:2611.33950v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: The values of causal effects and counterfactuals are typically only partially identified from observational data in the presence of unobserved confounding. With discretely-valued variables, under certain conditions, sharp bounds can be derived by solving one linear program. This is then computationally tractable for many causal questions. In this paper, for every diagram in which each confounded component has at most two hidden causes, we give necessary and sufficient conditions for the sharp bounds to be equal to the optimum of one linear program for every (positive) input probability table. This algorithm is implemented in a new Python package, called "partialid", that allows users to compose assumptions, queries, and data to obtain sharp bounds in a computationally tractable manner.
authors: Alexis Bellot

title: BReD: Block Replay Dithering for Stable Low-Bit EMA Optimizer States
summary: arXiv:2611.33951v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Low-bit storage of optimizer states can substantially reduce the memory footprint of large-scale training. In practice, however, these states are not quantized once: at every training step, they are dequantized, updated, requantized, and written back. This iterative quantization pipeline can destabilize training. We identify a failure mode behind this instability: for states updated via exponential moving averages (EMAs), quantization errors are recursively fed into subsequent updates. As a result, biased errors accumulate over time while high-variance errors are amplified, particularly when the EMA decay factor is close to 1. To address this error accumulation, we propose BReD (Block Replay Dithering), a method that reduces rounding bias and controls rounding variance during quantization. BReD adapts classical subtractive dithering to optimizer-state quantization by combining deterministic seed replay with block-wise shared dither values, avoiding auxiliary random-tensor storage and per-element dither values generation. Across the default pretraining settings (five optimizers at 120M; AdamW and Muon at 1.1B and 3.4B model) and supervised fine-tuning (AdamW and Muon at 7B model), 4-bit BReD closely matches training with full-precision optimizer states, with PPL shifts $\leq0.5$ in pretraining and $\leq0.2$ in fine-tuning and average downstream performance changes within 0.7 points. Moreover, 3-bit BReD preserves stable convergence in the evaluated settings, offering a more aggressive alternative. Our implementation of BReD is available at: https://github.com/ZhanHeshen/BReD
authors: Heshen Zhan, Youhan Huang, Yunke Peng, Yao Wang, Linghui Kong, Ziwei Zhu, Qingyu Han, Yaoyuan Wang, Congliang Chen, Ruoyu Sun

title: DuoMI: Dual Mutual Information Regularization for Expert Reuse in Looped Transformers
summary: arXiv:2611.33952v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We introduce Dual Mutual Information Regularization (DuoMI), a method for regulating expert routing across rounds in looped mixture-of-experts (MoE) Transformers. When two rounds of computation share an expert pool, their routers may favor different expert subsets, limiting the reuse of individual expert parameters across rounds. Even when aggregate expert usage is identical across rounds, we would still prefer each token to retain some experts while switching to others. DuoMI addresses both aspects of routing: it uses round-level marginal mutual information to limit the dependence of aggregate expert usage on the round, and token-level conditional mutual information to penalize average cross-round routing changes that fall outside a target interval. During training, DuoMI computes differentiable penalties from soft routing distributions over all experts. It adds no model parameters and leaves sparse Top-$k$ routing strategy unchanged at inference. On a looped OLMoE backbone in which paired adjacent layers share experts, DuoMI improves the average score across $15$ downstream tasks from $50.08\%$ to $51.82\%$, a gain of $1.74$ percentage points over the looped baseline.
authors: Xinlai Kang, Zhenhe Wu, Haoyu Wang, Weihua He, Yaping Jin, Jie Hu, Hanting Chen

title: RefMix: Expanding Endpoint Proposals for Diversity-Preserving Reward Fine-Tuning
summary: arXiv:2611.33957v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Online forward matching aligns flow-based generative models by repeatedly generating, rewarding, and fitting model-produced endpoints. However, this behavior creates an on-policy feedback loop: as high-reward modes become increasingly favored, alternative modes become less likely to appear in subsequent training pools, progressively reducing visual diversity. We introduce RefMix, a reference-assisted endpoint proposal strategy that addresses this limitation by injecting alternative candidates into the training pool while retaining the original task reward and forward matching objective. In particular, RefMix uses a reference model during early high-noise steps to expose alternative visual modes, followed by the current reward-tuned model for endpoint completion. Across state-of-the-art online forward matching methods, RefMix consistently improves visual diversity while preserving task reward performance. Controlled inference experiments further demonstrate that training-time endpoint exposure is critical to improve reward--diversity trade-offs, beyond the impact of reference-assisted inference. By rethinking how training endpoints are proposed, RefMix achieves up to 44% higher diversity over forward matching baselines at comparable reward levels.
authors: Jaemin Kim, Christian Simon, Dongseok Shim, Wei-Yao Wang, Qiyu Wu, Masato Ishii, Shusuke Takahashi, Jong Chul Ye, Yuki Mitsufuji

title: DLaR: Dynamic Stochasticity Control for Latent Reasoning in Large Language Models
summary: arXiv:2611.33962v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Latent reasoning enables LLMs to operate in continuous embedding space, yet existing methods suffer from deterministic inference that precludes exploration of diverse reasoning paths. While recent approaches inject stochasticity to restore exploration, we identify two fundamental limitations: \textit{uniform stochasticity} across all steps is suboptimal, and unconstrained perturbations disrupt reasoning coherence. We propose Dynamic Stochasticity Control for Latent Reasoning (DLaR), a framework with two complementary mechanisms that operate at different temporal granularities within the GRPO reinforcement learning framework. At the token level, Adaptive Stochasticity Modulation (ASM) dynamically adjusts perturbation intensity at each latent step based on a confidence-entropy fusion signal, increasing exploration when the model is uncertain and preserving stability when confident. At the training level, Training-Aware Stochasticity Tuning (TAST) progressively decays the base stochasticity level following a curriculum schedule. Through this dual-level design, DLaR establishes a hierarchical exploration-exploitation strategy that operates at both token and training levels. Extensive experiments on four in-distribution and three out-of-distribution mathematical reasoning benchmarks demonstrate that DLaR achieves the highest average performance across model scales, reaching 27.9%/50.6% Pass@1/Pass@8 on Llama-3.2-1B and 46.8%/68.2% on Qwen2.5-1.5B. Code: \href{https://github.com/xiaocen-luo/DLaR}{https://github.com/xiaocen-luo/DLaR}.
authors: Xiaocheng Luo, Peng Xu, Zaifu Zhan, Xiangyu Duan

title: Fine-Tuning Without Gradients? Closed-Form, LLM-Written Classifiers on a Frozen Encoder
summary: arXiv:2611.33972v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Can a classifier computed in closed form on a frozen encoder match gradient fine-tuning? We present closed-form weight-space programming (WSP): a large language model (LLM), used as a design assistant, writes programs that read a frozen masked language model through cloze-style prompt templates at several layers, fit closed-form heads (shrinkage discriminant analysis, kernel ridge regression and the encoder's label-word prior) on labelled data, and select among a pool of candidate heads by cross-fitting. No gradient is computed and no encoder weight changes. We instantiate the framework on RoBERTa-large. On 11 development datasets with 512 to 8,192 training labels, WSP is ahead of full fine-tuning (FT) and LoRA at every label budget (by 0.3 to 0.6 points on average; the registered non-inferiority tests pass) and within 0.5 points of prompt-based fine-tuning (PFT); these datasets also shaped the recipe. With fewer labels its lead over FT and LoRA grows: 1.2 to 3.5 points with 64 and 128 labels, and 3.8 to 5.3 points in the few-shot setting of 16 labels per class, where WSP is again within half a point of PFT on the development datasets. On six held-out datasets, WSP stays ahead of LoRA and within half a point of FT on average, although with six datasets no registered test passes, and PFT is ahead, by 1.30 points with 8,192 labels. WSP never collapses and is deterministic, but it needs one encoder pass per template (17 here). We report all eight recipe versions, every decision that saw test results, and 27 ideas that did not help.
authors: Md Nasir Uddin, Musa Tur Farazi, Soumik Bhattacharjee, Tishna Sabrina, Chowdhury Mohammad Rakin Haider

title: Kolpona: An Agentic Framework with Gradient-Free Neuron Programming for RTL Generation
summary: arXiv:2611.33973v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Open-weight large language models (LLMs) for register-transfer level (RTL) design are usually improved by fine-tuning on curated Verilog corpora, which needs large sets of verified designs and GPU training. We present Kolpona, an agentic framework that improves such models without gradient training. Its first component is neuron programming, a new form of weight-space programming (WSP) that writes single neurons in closed form into the weights to remove failure habits found on practice tasks, and keeps each edit only when testbench results on fresh tasks favour it. At inference time, tool-using agents propose designs, and a label-free selection stage delivers one design per task from the specification, the candidates and their simulations alone. On Qwen3.5-4B, edits to 16 neurons raise the VerilogEval v2 pass@1 of the model alone from 31.7% to 55.4%, and the full framework reaches 77.6%. On Qwen3.8-27B, Kolpona lifts pass@1 from 73.1% to 94.9% on VerilogEval v2 and from 66.0% to 92.0% on RTLLM v2.1 on a single 32 GB GPU, above every published system in our comparison. The RTL edits also carry over to Python and raise the pass@1 of the 4B model alone from 84.8% to 91.5% on HumanEval+ and from 67.7% to 77.5% on MBPP+.
authors: Musa Tur Farazi, Md Nasir Uddin, Soumik Bhattacharjee, Tishna Sabrina, Chowdhury Mohammad Rakin Haider

title: Quaternion-Tucker ZigZag Networks: Halving Transformer Backbone Parameters and Enabling Exact 2D Zero-Loss Continual Scaling
summary: arXiv:2611.33983v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Standard Transformers allocate independent dense weight matrices to every feed-forward network (FFN) layer, coupling parameters linearly with depth (O(L)) and discarding prior compute when scaling capacity. Conversely, weight-tied Looped Transformers decouple depth from parameters (O(1)) but enforce time-homogeneous updates. We formulate the L-layer FFN stack as a 3D Tensor Cuboid and introduce QuatTucker-ZigZagGPT, unifying: (1) 4D Quaternion Hamilton GEMMs in bfloat16 (4x FFN compression), (2) 64x64 Block-Diagonal Tucker SwiGLU Cores for depth-specific rotations over a shared basis, (3) Braided ZigZag Diamond Routing (L0 -> L2 -> L1 -> L3) for zero-FLOP top-down refinement, and (4) Exact 2D Zero-Loss Continual Scaling in both width and depth. We also introduce Annealed Gated Bounce-Back Scaffolding (GatedBounce), which self-distills to 0.0% inference overhead. Across algorithmic tasks (8-bit Parity, 56-seed routing ablations, Mod-53 Grokking) and language modeling (TinyStories, FineWeb-Edu), our model outperforms standard Transformers at 2x-7.6x compression. On A100, QuatTucker-ZigZagGPT-12 (39.0M backbone) beats StandardGPT-12 (85.0M backbone) at 5/5 controlled checkpoints. Continually scaling one lineage across 6.00B tokens via zero-loss width growth (rank 6144 -> 8192), two bit-exact depth expansions (L = 12 -> 16 -> 20, 70.9M backbone, max_diff = 0.000000), and WSD cooldown reaches 3.3582 FineWeb-Edu loss (28.74 PPL) and 44.75% full-split zero-shot accuracy across 16,955 questions (ARC-Easy, HellaSwag, WinoGrande, BoolQ), matching GPT-3 Small (125M, 300B tokens) at 50x fewer tokens.
authors: Shubham Barmase

title: MolGPAO: Molecular Generative Pre-trained Autoregressive Octree with Speculative Decoding and Sub-Millisecond Seam Healing for 3D Molecules
summary: arXiv:2611.33985v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Autoregressive generation over adaptive 3D octrees (Uni-3DAR) offers an intrinsic $O(N \log N)$ sparsity advantage over dense $O(N^2)$ equivariant diffusion and flow models on large drug-like molecules, yet lags in geometric equilibrium, closed-shell valence stability, and property fidelity due to Morton-seam coordinate jumps, leaf-heavy compute with root-count trapping, and target-shortcut collapse in internal critics. We introduce MolGPAO (Molecular Generative Pre-trained Autoregressive Octree), a standalone 3D octree architecture and single-output speculative tree-decoding engine using zero external surrogates, zero reinforcement learning, and zero inference-time MLIP relaxation.
